author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify the structural components of DNA — the sugar-phosphate backbone, the four nitrogenous bases, and the hydrogen bonds between base pairs — and describe how they assemble into the double helix.

Students will apply the complementary base-pairing rules (A with T, G with C) to determine the sequence of one strand given the sequence of the other, and explain why these specific pairings occur (two hydrogen bonds for A-T, three for G-C).
Students will describe the antiparallel orientation of the two strands of DNA and explain how the 5'-to-3' directionality of each sugar-phosphate backbone determines this arrangement.
Students will trace the action of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork, identifying which enzyme performs which function.

Students will explain why DNA replication produces a leading strand synthesized continuously and a lagging strand synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, relating this asymmetry to the unidirectional 5'-to-3' activity of DNA polymerase on antiparallel templates.
Students will articulate why DNA replication is described as semiconservative, and predict the composition of daughter molecules after one and two rounds of replication.

modules.moduleName: The DNA Double Helix: Structure and Components
modules.description: An examination of the three-dimensional structure of DNA, including the sugar-phosphate backbone, nitrogenous bases, and base-pairing interactions that stabilize the double helix.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the sugar-phosphate backbone and the four nitrogenous bases in DNA
Explain how complementary base pairing (A-T and G-C) occurs and the hydrogen bonding patterns involved
Describe the antiparallel orientation of DNA strands and the 5'-to-3' directionality
Visualize how these components combine to form the double helix geometry
instructions: Observe the DNA double helix model as it appears and rotates before you.
Listen to the narration explaining each structural component.
Note how the bases pair across the interior of the helix and how the backbones spiral outward.
Pay attention to the directional arrows indicating 5'-to-3' orientation on each strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the rotating DNA helix model to establish the overall 3D structure and establish the context for examining individual components.
clips.narration: The DNA molecule is a double helix, composed of two antiparallel strands that spiral around a common axis. Each strand is made up of a sugar-phosphate backbone with nitrogenous bases projecting inward. The bases from one strand pair with bases on the other strand, held together by hydrogen bonds.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the sugar-phosphate backbone with a label to draw student attention to this critical structural component and emphasize directionality.
clips.narration: The sugar-phosphate backbone forms the structural core of each DNA strand. Deoxyribose sugar molecules are linked together by phosphodiester bonds. Importantly, each backbone has directionality: one end has a free phosphate group at the 5' carbon, and the other end has a free hydroxyl group at the 3' carbon. The two strands are antiparallel, meaning they run in opposite directions — one strand goes 5' to 3' while the other runs 3' to 5'.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the nitrogenous bases and their roles, highlighting their position within the helix and their pairing specificity.
clips.narration: Four nitrogenous bases make up the variable part of DNA: adenine and guanine are larger purines with two fused rings, while thymine and cytosine are smaller pyrimidines with a single ring. These bases project inward from the sugar-phosphate backbone and pair specifically with bases on the opposite strand. Adenine always pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds, and guanine always pairs with cytosine via three hydrogen bonds. This complementary base pairing is fundamental to DNA structure and function.

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasize the hydrogen bonding network that maintains base pairing, showing how this property enables both stability and the ability to separate during replication.
clips.narration: The bases are held in their paired configuration by hydrogen bonds — weak interactions that form between the electronegative atoms in the bases. Adenine-thymine base pairs form two hydrogen bonds, providing moderate stability, while guanine-cytosine base pairs form three hydrogen bonds, making them slightly more stable. These hydrogen bonds are individually weak but collectively strong enough to hold the double helix together, yet weak enough to be broken during DNA replication.

clips.changeMeaning: Synthesize all components into the complete double helix geometry, with the model continuing to rotate to show the 3D spatial arrangement.
clips.narration: The antiparallel strands wind around each other to form the characteristic double helix shape. The bases stack on top of each other inside the helix, while the sugar-phosphate backbones form the external spiral structure. This geometry is constrained by the molecular properties of the components — the helix pitch, radius, and rise per base pair are all determined by the chemistry of the bases and the flexibility of the backbone. The result is one of biology's most elegant molecular structures.

modules.description: A detailed walkthrough of semiconservative DNA replication, showing how enzymes unwind the helix and synthesize new strands asymmetrically, and explaining how each daughter molecule retains one parental strand.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the action of helicase and single-strand binding proteins at the replication fork
Explain how DNA polymerase synthesizes complementary strands and why it can only extend in the 5' to 3' direction
Distinguish between leading strand and lagging strand synthesis, and describe Okazaki fragments
Understand why DNA replication is semiconservative and predict daughter molecule composition
instructions: Follow the animation as the DNA helicase unwinds the double helix.
Observe how single-strand binding proteins stabilize the exposed strands.
Watch as DNA polymerase synthesizes the leading and lagging strands.
Note how DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
Trace the final products to understand semiconservative replication.

components.text:
Semiconservative Replication:
Each daughter molecule contains
one parental strand and one new strand

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the replication fork model and establish the overall enzymatic choreography that drives DNA replication.
clips.narration: DNA replication begins when the double helix must be copied. The process requires several key enzymes working in concert. At the replication fork, where the DNA unwinds, helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, separating the two strands. Single-strand binding proteins then coat the exposed strands to prevent them from re-annealing or forming secondary structures. DNA polymerase then synthesizes new complementary strands using each parental strand as a template.

clips.changeMeaning: Show helicase positioned at the replication fork, beginning to separate the strands. Visualize the unwinding action.
clips.narration: Helicase is a molecular machine that uses energy from ATP hydrolysis to unwind the double helix. It breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs and separates the two strands, moving along the DNA in the 5' to 3' direction. This creates a replication fork — a Y-shaped structure where the helix transitions from double-stranded to single-stranded DNA. Without helicase, the cell would have no way to access the genetic information needed for replication.

clips.changeMeaning: Add SSB protein at the single-stranded region, showing how it stabilizes and protects the unwound DNA.
clips.narration: Single-strand binding proteins, or SSB proteins, rapidly bind to the exposed single strands behind helicase. These proteins prevent the separated strands from re-annealing with each other and also protect them from nucleases and other cellular factors. By keeping the strands apart and extended, SSB proteins allow DNA polymerase access to the template strands. SSB proteins are released once DNA polymerase has synthesized the complementary strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Show DNA polymerase positioned on the leading strand template, synthesizing a continuous complementary strand in the 5' to 3' direction.
clips.narration: DNA polymerase synthesizes the new strand complementary to the template strand. Critically, DNA polymerase can only extend a growing strand in the 5' to 3' direction — it adds nucleotides to the 3' hydroxyl group. On the leading strand template, which runs 3' to 5' toward the replication fork, DNA polymerase moves continuously in the same direction as the replication fork, synthesizing a continuous new strand. This is the leading strand synthesis.

clips.changeMeaning: Illustrate the lagging strand template and show multiple DNA polymerase enzymes synthesizing short Okazaki fragments in the direction away from the replication fork.
clips.narration: The lagging strand template runs 5' to 3' toward the replication fork. Since DNA polymerase can only synthesize in the 5' to 3' direction, it cannot move continuously away from the replication fork on this template. Instead, DNA polymerase must synthesize the new strand in short segments called Okazaki fragments, each 100 to 1000 nucleotides long in prokaryotes, moving away from the replication fork. This discontinuous synthesis is the defining characteristic of lagging strand replication.

clips.changeMeaning: Show DNA ligase joining Okazaki fragments together, completing the synthesis of the lagging strand.
clips.narration: After DNA polymerase has synthesized all the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, gaps remain between the fragments. DNA ligase seals these gaps by forming phosphodiester bonds between the 3' hydroxyl of one fragment and the 5' phosphate of the next fragment. Ligase uses energy from ATP to create these covalent bonds, joining the fragments into a continuous strand. The lagging strand is now complete and covalently intact.

clips.changeMeaning: Display the semiconservative replication concept, showing how parental strands are conserved in daughter molecules and the implications for multiple rounds of replication.
clips.narration: DNA replication is semiconservative because each daughter molecule contains one strand from the parent molecule and one newly synthesized strand. This was proven in the Meselson-Stahl experiment using heavy and light isotopes of nitrogen. After one round of replication, both daughter molecules are hybrid — half parental, half new. After two rounds of replication, one molecule is fully new while the other is still half parental. This pattern confirms that each parental strand serves as a template for exactly one new strand.
